The empirical scope is fairly broad, covering class-level generalization, domain/feature shift, and label-skew personalization across many standard datasets, with comparisons to several recent federated prompt-learning baselines.
The reported results are promising, especially the harmonic-mean performance in base-to-novel evaluation, the DomainNet/Office-Caltech average, and the CIFAR-10/100 personalization results.
weaknesses: The central design is not sufficiently isolated experimentally. The paper lacks key ablations such as local-only MMA, FedAvg over full adapters, sharing different adapter components, visual-only/text-only adapters, different insertion layers, and different bottleneck sizes.

The baseline set is incomplete for the main claim. Comparisons are mostly against prompt-based PFL methods, but adapter/PEFT baselines such as federated CLIP-Adapter, Tip-Adapter-style adaptation, LoRA/FedPEFT variants, and centralized or local adapter upper bounds are needed.

Several claims are stronger than the tables support. For example, the text says pFedMMA achieves the highest novel accuracy and matches the top base accuracy on the averaged seven-dataset setting, but Table 1 shows CLIP slightly higher on novel and PromptFL much higher on base.

Reproducibility and reporting are weak: the manuscript refers to an Appendix that is not included, gives inconsistent dataset/client counts, provides no standard deviations despite averaging over seeds, and gives limited detail on hyperparameter tuning and baseline fairness.

The communication-efficiency claim is asserted rather than demonstrated. There are no parameter counts, transmitted-byte comparisons, compute/memory measurements, or scaling experiments with realistic partial participation beyond the CIFAR setup.

The FL/privacy framing is underdeveloped. Sharing adapter projections can still leak information about client distributions, but the paper does not discuss threat models, secure aggregation, differential privacy, or privacy-utility tradeoffs.

The writing and presentation need polishing, with typos, formatting issues, small figures/tables, and inconsistencies such as saying nine datasets or six CLIP datasets while the abstract and tables imply eleven datasets and seven CLIP-style datasets.
